stem: A 4-year-old girl is brought in by her mother, a pharmacy technician, after noticing a firm, slowly enlarging lump on the child's neck over the past three weeks. The child has been otherwise playful, with only mild intermittent low-grade fevers noted by touch, no documented true fever. The mother initially assumed it was a reactive lymph node from a recent minor throat infection, but it hasn't shrunk with a course of amoxicillin prescribed for presumed bacterial lymphadenitis. There is no known TB contact in the household, though the mother mentions a family friend recently completed TB treatment. Fine-needle aspiration of the node was performed and sent for molecular testing, which was positive for M. tuberculosis. No prior TB treatment, no known drug-resistant contact. Exam: firm, mildly tender 2.5 cm left cervical lymph node, no overlying skin changes, no other lymphadenopathy, lungs clear.

patient.occupation: not applicable (household occupational context: mother works as a pharmacy technician)
patient.social_history: Lives with mother; a family friend recently completed a course of TB treatment
patient.presenting_complaint: Slowly enlarging, firm cervical lymph node unresponsive to a course of antibiotics
patient.exam_findings: Firm, mildly tender 2.5 cm left cervical lymph node, no overlying skin changes, no other lymphadenopathy, lungs clear
patient.prior_treatment: One course of amoxicillin for presumed bacterial lymphadenitis, no improvement; no prior TB treatment

distractors: Reactive cervical lymphadenopathy from a recent minor throat infection, reinforced by lack of response ruling out the wrong specific antibiotic rather than the wrong diagnostic category
The family friend's completed TB treatment treated as reassuring (successfully treated) rather than prompting consideration of a transmission window before treatment completion
ntep_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the lymph node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
who_correct_actions: Perform upfront molecular testing (NAAT) directly on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen (the lymph node aspirate) as the first-line microbiological tool, rather than anchoring the workup around culture and histology as the primary reference standard.
us_correct_actions: Anchor the diagnostic workup for this extrapulmonary presentation around culture and histology as the reference standard, treating molecular testing as a general, conditional adjunct rather than the upfront first-line tool for extrapulmonary specimens.
critical_error_conditions: Attributing the persistent neck mass entirely to inadequate antibiotic coverage and prescribing a second antibiotic course rather than pursuing tissue/aspirate sampling for a specific diagnosis
expected_divergence_points: Whether upfront molecular testing on the accessible extrapulmonary specimen is the first-line diagnostic tool or culture/histology remains the anchoring reference standard
